abstract: Recent works have proposed semi-device-independent frameworks to certify non-stabilizerness, but the complexity of the stabilizer polytope makes these methods infeasible beyond a few qubits. In this work, we address this limitation by moving to partially characterized measurements in the context of worst-case random access codes. We first establish a simple condition, which we term the stabilizer pigeonhole criterion, that certifies non-stabilizerness in $m$-qubit pure states, and show how it can be applied to reduced states. As an application, we certify magic in $W$ states of arbitrary size using only eight preparations and three single-qubit measurement settings. Motivated by recent work on the stabilizer marginal problem, we then construct prepare-and-measure correlations generated by global $m$-qubit quantum states for which every $k$-qubit marginal lies inside the stabilizer polytope, yet the combined correlations cannot be reproduced by any global stabilizer mixture. Finally, we derive analytical upper and lower bounds on the worst-case bias attainable with mixed stabilizer preparations in an $m$-qubit random access code with $n$ Pauli measurements. For the complete set of $4^m-1$ non-identity Pauli measurements, we show that the optimal quantum and mixed-stabilizer biases both scale as $2^{-3m/2}$, and that their ratio is asymptotically bounded by a constant ($\lesssim 1.85$), showing that in this setting, magic in the preparations alone yields at most a constant-factor advantage over stabilizer mixtures.
